content.text:
Happy to. And I'd push on the framing a little before answering it, because I think the binary is where the difficulty actually hides.

## "Done" and "needs judgment" aren't two ends of one axis

A task can be fully done *and* have contained judgment calls — they just got made. A task can need a judgment call before a single line is written. So the useful unit isn't the work item, it's the **decisions inside it**. Every item contains a set of decisions, and the skill is sorting each one into three buckets: decide silently, decide and announce, don't decide. Most land in the first bucket. If I'm routinely putting things in the third, I'm not delegating back — I'm just making you do the work with extra steps.

## The filter that does the most work: ignorance vs. underdetermination

Before anything else, I ask whether the answer *exists somewhere I can reach*. In the code, the tests, the git history, a doc, a convention in a neighboring file. If it does, I don't have a judgment call — I have homework. Go look. I think the large majority of "should I check with you?" impulses are actually this, and asking is just a way of outsourcing search.

Only when nobody has decided yet — the answer isn't anywhere because it doesn't exist — is it a real judgment call. Then two more tests:

**Does it diverge?** Do the plausible readings produce materially different work? If both roads end at the same code, pick one and shut up about it.

**What does being wrong cost?** Two variables, and reversibility is the obvious one. The underrated one is **detectability**. A wrong guess that fails loudly — test breaks, build fails — is nearly free, because the system catches it. A wrong guess that produces plausible-looking output nobody inspects is expensive *even when it's technically easy to reverse*, because the reversal never gets triggered.

The slugify work happens to have one of each tier, which is handy:

- The redundant `.trim()` in the spec — underdetermined, but *converges*. Same output either way. Honestly I could have said nothing.
- Non-string input — diverges, but fails loudly the moment anyone passes a number. Pick a behavior, note it, move.
- Unicode — diverges, and here's the thing, it fails *quietly*. `café` → `caf-` ships, looks fine in the diff, looks fine in the tests I wrote, and surfaces months later as somebody's broken URL. That silence is most of why I raised it rather than quietly picking ASCII.

Note that none of those were blocking. Blocking is reserved for "proceeding under any assumption could be unsafe or make the work useless if wrong" — a destructive migration, an outward-facing action. Everything else gets a decision plus a stated assumption.

## On "done," the evidence ladder matters more than the claim

Weakest: I wrote it and it looks right. That's worth approximately nothing. Then: it runs. Then: tests fail before and pass after — and the *before* is load-bearing, which is why I ran the suite and reported 6 failures instead of just handing you test code. A test that never failed proves nothing except that it's a test. Strongest: it holds on inputs I didn't pick.

But here's the ceiling. Every rung of that ladder certifies conformance to **my reading of the spec**. None of them can certify that my reading was right. The spec is a lossy encoding of what you actually want, and tests passing is fully compatible with having confidently misread it.

Which is why your instinct to stop and look at tests before implementation is doing more work than it might appear. It's not mainly a correctness checkpoint — it's an **intent checkpoint**, placed at the cheapest possible moment. The tests *are* the spec made executable, so reading them is the fastest way to catch a misread. Once the implementation exists, the same misread costs more to find and more to undo.

## What I'd actually commit to

I'd claim done only when I can state five things: what the goal was, what I did, what evidence I have, what I assumed, and what I deliberately left out. If I can't fill in all five, I'm not done — I'm optimistic. And partial work reported as complete is the worst outcome available, worse than visibly unfinished work, because it poisons every future completion report you get from me.

Two corollaries I'd hold myself to:

**Escalation comes with a recommendation.** "Which do you want?" is lazy. "I'd go ASCII-only because most slug consumers are URLs; say the word if you want Unicode" is answerable in one syllable and still leaves the call with you.

**Scaling down scope is your call, not mine.** If one part is genuinely blocked, I finish everything else in full and say plainly what I left and why — rather than quietly shipping a smaller thing and calling it done.

## The part I'm least sure about

My own uncertainty is poorly calibrated. I can be confidently wrong, which makes "do I *feel* unsure?" a bad trigger — it's exactly silent in the cases that matter most. So I'd rather lean on structural triggers that don't require introspection: does the spec mention this case at all? does any existing test pin it? is there a convention already in this repo? Those are checkable facts.

And there's a real cost to the opposite failure. Three flagged ambiguities on a ten-line function is pushing it. Past some density, caveats stop being useful and start being a way of making you do the thinking while I get credit for thoroughness.

Where would you want the line drawn differently? I'm curious in particular whether you'd rather I bias toward stating assumptions and continuing, or toward stopping more often than I did here.
